articles.title: Three killed, four injured in shooting at Detroit, Michigan, strip club
articles.summary: Police say the US shooting followed an altercation at an after-hours venue, and four people are in hospital.
articles.body:
Three people have been killed and four others injured in a shooting at an after-hours strip club in Detroit, Michigan in the United States, according to police.

Officers responding to the shooting shortly after 7:20am local time (11:20 GMT) on Sunday arrived within four minutes and found three people suffering from fatal gunshot wounds, Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison told reporters on Sunday morning.

Another four people – two men and two women in their 20s and 30s – were taken to area hospitals with injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

The three people killed, who police said were all over the age of 30, have not yet been identified.

Bettison said the shooting followed an altercation at the club, located on a mostly residential street.

“A fight occurred, an altercation occurred, and as a result individuals decided to settle it with gun violence,” he said.

Police have not announced any arrests, but Bettison said investigators had developed leads and there was no ongoing danger to the public.

The location was already known to police, who had received seven calls related to the address since the beginning of the year. Bettison said there was also an investigation into the address.

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield said the city would work to crack down on illegal after-hours operations, whether they were being run out of homes or businesses.

Sheffield said authorities would do “everything we can” to prevent such operations from taking place in Detroit’s communities and neighbourhoods.

articles.title: Tourism tax needs to be revisited in Wales, expert says
articles.summary: Anglesey, Conwy and Gwynedd councils have all put a pause on introducing the nightly tourist tax.
articles.body:
Wales' tourism tax needs to be more flexible, an expert has said.

Last week, Anglesey council rejected introducing the visitor levy for now, over concerns for its tourism industry, while Gwynedd and Conwy councils both postponed making any decision on the nightly fee.

It is down to local authorities to decide whether they want to introduce the Welsh government legislation, which means that from 2027 a fixed price can be charged per person, per night , and applies to both adults and children.

The Welsh government said the legislation allowed for decisions to be taken at a local level, with councils able to introduce the levy "to support investment in tourism services and facilities".

A tourism tax, or levy, is a charge which would need to be paid by anyone staying overnight in any area which introduces it.

The idea is that it covers, or contributes to, the costs which authorities face as a result of the tourism industry.

If a local authority decides to introduce the tourism tax, fees for people staying in hostels, shared rooms and tent pitches would be 75p + VAT per person per night, while most other types of accommodation would be charged at £1.30 + VAT.

But according to Dr Linda Osti, senior tourism lecturer at Bangor University, decisions on how much is charged, and how a levy is brought in, should be made on a more local level instead of a one-size-fits-all approach.

"It's one legislation for every county and and it's applied at county level, when we should think about sub-county level," she said.

"Geographically, if we think about Gwynedd....we cannot have the same levy on Eryri or Porthmadog. The same legislation cannot work for Cardiff, or in Anglesey, on the coast.

"There are different visitors, there are also different conditions."

Osti also suggested there was a "mistrust" from tourism businesses on how local authorities would spend money generated from tourism tax, compared to places like the Italian alps where decisions are made through smaller co-operatives.

Earlier this month, it was announced that regional mayors in England would gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy on overnight stays for visitors.

Osti, who co-authored a 2024 report for the Welsh government studying how visitor levies worked in other countries , said: "If we compare what we know from England, which is very little at the moment, it appears to be much more flexible.

"So local authorities can decide the percentage to charge and whether to introduce exemptions, and it seems they may also decide for how many nights, and whether to charge children or not.

"I wish Wales would go back and think about flexibility and revisit the legislation."

On Thursday, Anglesey council confirmed it would not introduce the so-called tourism tax for now, "given the challenges already facing its tourism industry".

It said a public consultation received more than 2,000 responses, including from residents, businesses and tourism stakeholders, with concerns voiced about increased costs for visitors, and the island's "competitiveness" as a holiday destination.

Meanwhile, Cyngor Gywnedd agreed to delay its decision over the levy so more analysis could be done of almost 7,000 responses to its consultation - a number it said was "much higher" than other areas.

The local authority said initial figures showed a mixed reaction to the proposals, with more support from residents but higher levels of opposition from visitors and businesses.

In Conwy, council members also chose to defer a decision on implementing the levy until "further evidence and practical experience are available".

It said concerns from consultations included fears over reduced bookings, shorter stays and reduced visitor spend at a time when local businesses are facing economic pressures.

Bethan Evans, of family-run business Dolgamedd caravan park in Dolgellau, Gwynedd, is one of those in support of introducing a tourism tax in the county to help areas cope with busy roads and car parks at peak times.

She said she was "disappointed" that councils appeared to be "scared of a noisy, selfish minority" opposing the fee, and described the 75p per night levy for people camping as "nothing" compared to the rubbish that some visitors left behind at the site.

"You get people [with] brand new tents who can't be bothered to put a wet tent back in the car so they try and dump them in our bins, which we pay for," she said.

"There is such a lot of that happening, and the amount of food waste is just incredible. So it's ridiculous saying they can't afford it, oh yes they can."

But she added: "Some people are wonderful, and those people are happy to pay the tax. We want people who respect the area, who are willing to pay the tax, so that's the kind of tourist I'd like."

Nicky Williamson, of the Professional Association of Self-Caterers (PASC) UK Cymru, described the pause on introducing the levy across the three counties as a "welcome victory for common sense and for listening to the evidence".

She said: "Tourism businesses across Wales have been clear about the pressures they are already facing, and the response to these consultations shows the strength of concern about adding another cost to Welsh holidays.

"This is simply the wrong time to introduce another cost for either businesses or visitors. We welcome councils listening to the evidence and urge others to do the same before taking decisions that could have long-term consequences for Wales' visitor economy."

So far, Cardiff council looks set to become the only local authority in Wales to introduce the visitor levy next year, according to the Welsh government .

From 28 September, those staying in the county must pay the levy on bookings made for 1 April 2027 onwards.

According to Osti, Cardiff is an example of where the current tourism tax legislation should work well, especially with business tourists who are less "price sensitive".

"Why would it work in Cardiff? Because it's a typical city destination. People tend to go to Cardiff for a few nights," she said.

"For two people, two nights, it's not even £10 extra when they're paying £100, £140, £160 per night for a double bedroom.

"So it would work for Cardiff and then Cardiff can easily organise events as Manchester and Liverpool did in the past... they could do very good things with the charge."

The visitor levy came about as part of a co-operation deal signed between Labour and Plaid Cymru in 2021, with the legislation published in 2024.

Officials said they wanted the tax to be simple to understand, so the same rate will be paid for adults and children - although under 18s will be exempt from the 75p rate.

Local authorities decide not only whether to implement the levy, but also how the money generated is spent, according to local needs.

This is ring-fenced in their budgets for specific things, like promoting tourism, promoting the Welsh language, and improving infrastructure or services used by visitors.

While the current fee per night is fixed, councils could also charge more in future if they go through a consultation process and give 12 months' notice.

Stays of more than 31 nights will not be taxed, and neither will people forced into temporary accommodation or people in homeless hostels.

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "It is for local authorities to decide if they want to introduce a levy in their area following consultation with their communities.

"Cardiff, for example, will implement a levy from April 2027, generating revenues to be re-invested in and around the city that will further enhance the experience for visitors."

articles.title: ‘Please fight’: How an elderly woman’s eviction put Spain’s housing crisis in the spotlight
articles.summary: If there’s one name on people’s lips in Spain this week it’s Maricarmen. The eviction of the 87-year-old from her home has sparked a huge wave of spontaneous solidarity in various cities and drawn attention to one of the most pressing problems facing the country: access to housing.
articles.body: If there’s one name on people’s lips in Spain this week it’s Maricarmen. The eviction of the 87-year-old from her home has sparked a huge wave of spontaneous solidarity in various cities and drawn attention to one of the most pressing problems facing the country: access to housing. Tens of thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest Maricarmen’s eviction. Some demonstrators camped overnight in Puerta del Sol, where more people, including families of several generations, joined them Sunday, according to the Associated Press. Protesters are demanding stronger tenant protections and a ban on evictions when no other housing is available nearby. María del Carmen Abascal, known by her nickname Maricarmen, is a resident of Madrid’s El Retiro neighborhood who, until last Wednesday, lived in an apartment on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street. She had lived in that home for more than 70 years, her attorney, Beatriz Duro, told CNN. Her eviction, which shocked many, took place Wednesday despite the efforts of dozens of people who had waited outside her home since the previous night trying to prevent it. That afternoon, nearly 10,000 people, according to the Spanish government officials in Madrid, gathered in the capital to protest Maricarmen’s eviction, while also expressing their frustration over the growing difficulties in finding housing. These concerns and expressions of solidarity protests also took place in other cities such as Barcelona, Seville, and Valencia. Abascal is currently hospitalized at Gregorio Marañón Hospital, where she was taken on a stretcher immediately after being evicted from her apartment. She is expected to remain there for a couple of days, Duro said, while she awaits some medical tests. Abascal spoke to supporters via a video Friday after being transferred to the hospital and urged them to “keep fighting” for their homes. “I did not manage to defend my home, but I have fought so that others learn to fight for theirs,” she said. “My house has been my life. And now I have to leave it behind. But that does not mean I will not keep fighting.” “Please fight,” she told supporters. “I send you all a very big hug and thank you for everything.” Evicted after 70 years Abascal had lived in the same place since 1956. In this apartment, located near El Retiro Park, she grew up and lived with her parents until she inherited and took over their lease from them. It was an old-style lease under which she paid about $568 (500 euros) per month. However, everything changed when the real estate company Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión acquired ownership of the apartment building for $280,787 (247,000 euros) in March 2018. That’s when her ordeal began, as shortly afterward the new owner began demanding a rent that was up to four times higher—even though she receives a pension of only $1,478 (1,300 euros), the Madrid Tenants’ Union told CNN. Consequently, in March 2020, the property company filed a lawsuit seeking the termination of the lease, Duro said. Abascal won the case in the lower court, but the company appealed, and the Provincial Court ruled in its favor. Faced with this situation, Duro filed a petition for constitutional protection with the Constitutional Court and an appeal with the Supreme Court, but both were dismissed. At the same time, Urbagestión filed a lawsuit to enforce the termination of the lease and thus regain possession of the home, which resulted in up to four eviction attempts. In October 2025, Abascal’s defense team halted the eviction for four months thanks to a provision in the law that allows for this when the party seeking eviction is a legal entity, Duro said. In June 2026, when the second date was set, the eviction was suspended for nearly a month due to the tenant’s vulnerable situation—she had no alternative housing. Consequently, it was postponed again until July, but Duro appealed the decision once more. During this time and until the eviction took place, Abascal’s support network made significant efforts to negotiate with Urbagestión to find solutions that would prevent this outcome. Among other things, Duro noted that mediation was conducted through Casa 47, the state housing agency, to have them purchase the apartment and rent it to her at a more reasonable price. On Tuesday, before the eviction, an anonymous person offered to pay part of the rent. But the real estate company showed no interest in any of the proposed alternatives, her lawyer said. CNN has reached out to Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión for comment but has not yet received a response. Given this situation and with the eviction already carried out, Abascal’s prospects are not very promising. “The situation is desperate,” Duro said. “She has no housing alternative, (..) and she still has not received any kind of proposal or housing alternative from public authorities.” City Hall reported that, on Friday morning, the real estate company contacted the Madrid Municipal Housing and Land Agency (EMVS) to have the property included in the ReViVa Program—through which City Hall recovers vacant homes to introduce them into the rental market—and thus offer it to Abascal “on affordable terms.” However, the City Council has rejected this possibility, deeming the proposal unfeasible because it does not meet the program’s legal requirements. They have, however, offered the EMVS Rental Mediation Service so that the company and the tenant can negotiate during a meeting scheduled for Monday, with professionals acting as mediators. The housing crisis in Spain The difficulties in accessing housing—whether to buy or rent—are nothing new in Spain. Protests have multiplied in recent years, and pressure has mounted on both local authorities and the government led by President Pedro Sánchez. This discontent stems from rising housing prices and is felt particularly acutely in major cities. In Madrid, for example, rent has nearly doubled in a decade, rising from $14.55 (12.8 euros) per square meter in August 2016 to $26.49 (23.3 euros) in August 2026, according to data from the real estate website Idealista. As for home purchases, the price per square meter has risen by 227.9% in just 10 years—that is, from $3,229 (2,839 euros) per square meter in August 2016 to $7,361 (6,471 euros) in August of this year, according to Idealista. These prices stand in stark contrast to the country’s average annual salary, which in 2024 was around $33,596 (29,540 euros), according to data from the National Institute of Statistics. In other words, based on these figures, someone who decides to rent a 50-square-meter apartment in the capital will be spending about $15,894 (13,980 euros) a year on housing, which amounts to nearly half of the average salary. This financial burden compromises one’s ability to save and cover other expenses. UN-Habitat (the United Nations Human Settlements Program) estimates that, for rent to be considered affordable, less than 30% of one’s income should be spent on it. The Bank of Spain believes that a large part of this problem stems from a housing shortage that currently stands at around 755,000 homes and could reach one million by 2028. The political battle Given the magnitude of this eviction, the political class has not remained on the sidelines. This is not only because those defending Abascal have directly called them out, but also because politicians themselves have used this episode as a platform from which to defend themselves or attack others. Speaking at a Socialist Party rally in Madrid on Sunday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed Abascal directly: “I have a message for you, Maricarmen: the government is working around the clock to bring a Royal Decree on housing next Tuesday. And I ask parliamentary groups to make one last effort to have it validated in the National Parliament for Maricarmen,” according to the Associated Press. Abascal has previously criticized Sánchez and blamed him for her ordeal. “Does he not realize the quantity of evictions that there are daily?” she asked during an interview with Spain’s state broadcaster RTVE the day before she was forcibly removed from her home. “Does he not realize, or does he not want to realize?” The Spanish government maintains that it has attempted, through the Ministry of Housing and Casa 47, to purchase the home where Abascal lived in order to provide her with affordable rent. At the same time, it criticizes local and regional authorities for having done nothing to help her. The president of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, passed the buck back to the executive branch led by Sánchez, stating on Thursday morning that the eviction was carried out by National Police officers—“who are managed by the government”—in compliance with a law “that this government and its coalition partners have had eight years to amend if they disagreed with it.” For their part, the coalition government’s partners—the members of Sumar—are proposing to directly expropriate the home in question. Specifically, both the Second Vice President of the Spanish Government, Yolanda Díaz, and the Minister of Social Rights, Consumer Affairs, and the 2030 Agenda, Pablo Bustinduy, are pushing for the Royal Decree-Law on Housing to be approved at the next Council of Ministers meeting, which would freeze rent prices and halt evictions such as the one that took place on Wednesday.

articles.title: Florida Gators may or may not be ‘back,’ but one thing is certain, football is finally fun in The Swamp again
articles.summary: Jon Sumrall's Florida Gators crushed No. 4 Ole Miss and surged to 8th in the AP Poll, but the new coach says the beast hasn't fully awakened yet.
articles.body: December 5, 2009. I remember it like it was yesterday. It was the date of the SEC Championship, the supposed "Game of the Century" in college football. Florida vs. Alabama. Number one against number two. A rematch of last season's thriller between the two teams and a matchup thought to be a "de facto" national championship game. FLORIDA GATORS, OLE MISS REBELS FIND THEMSELVES IN GOOD OLD FASHIONED 'RESPECT OFF' AHEAD OF SATURDAY'S GAME It was also the night the Gators' budding dynasty came crumbling down before our very eyes. Oh sure, Florida would go on to eviscerate Cincinnati in the Sugar Bowl less than a month later, and they even managed to cobble together a few impressive seasons in the years since. JAMES MADISON COACH BILLY NAPIER CONTINUES SELF PITY TOUR, REFUSES TO TAKE ACCOUNTABILITY FOR PAST FAILURES But as far as being the nationally relevant powerhouse they had become under head coaches Steve Spurrier and Urban Meyer in the 90s and 2000s, those days were long gone. The Gators would stumble their way through myriad coaching searches, hiring flawed candidate after flawed candidate. If Florida landed a defensive wizard (Will Muschamp), the offense would suffer under his watch. Conversely, if the Gators nabbed an offensive guru (Dan Mullen), the defense would inevitably fail to live up to their end of the bargain. FLORIDA GATORS COACH JON SUMRALL SAYS HE WOULDN'T HAVE LEFT TULANE IF HE WASN'T ALLOWED TO COACH PLAYOFF TEAM And if they happened to get a guy who was a relentless recruiter (Billy Napier), neither side of the ball would look up to snuff. Big wins were short-lived, usually followed by a cataclysmic event that would tank any shot at a successful season after the fact. In 2015, the Gators welcomed a top-three Ole Miss team to The Swamp in an eerily similar scenario to Saturday's game, and handled them from the opening whistle. Just weeks later, rising second-year signal caller Will Grier would be suspended for testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs, and the Jim McElwain era was never able to replicate the magic of those first six games. COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING Five years later, during the fog of the COVID-19-shortened season of 2020, Florida had a legitimate championship-level offense under head coach Dan Mullen's tutelage, and even with a porous defense, were able to knock Georgia off its perch and take the inside track to the SEC Championship Game. A month after their win over their fiercest rival, the Gators lost as a three-touchdown favorite at home to LSU thanks to the now infamous "shoe toss" from defensive back Marco Wilson. HOW A PODCAST COMMUNITY HELPED RESTORE THE CONTROVERSIAL 'GATOR BAIT' CHANT FOR FLORIDA FOOTBALL TEAM Mullen was relieved of his duties as head coach less than a year afterwards. My point is that any time the Gators seemed to gain a foothold in the "we're back" conversation, something would jump up and drag them back to reality. I'm not sure if Saturday's domination over number four Ole Miss means the Gators are "back," but for the first time in a very long time, the picture is looking clearer than ever. The offense looks as dangerous as it did six years ago, when that aforementioned 2020 team ran roughshod over a 10-game SEC schedule thanks to the aerial assault provided by Kyle Trask, Kyle Pitts and Kadarius Toney, among others. And the crazy thing is, this year's offense might be deeper and even more balanced. Consider the fact that Florida had Eric Singleton Jr., Vernell Brown III and Bailey Stockton, three of their top four wideouts, all hobbled for large portions of the game, and still put up 52 points and nearly 500 yards of total offense against a top-five SEC team. That 2020 offense was lethal, but they couldn't run the ball as effectively and certainly didn't have a tailback of Jadan Baugh's magnitude. The defense was the Achilles heel of that COVID-19-year team, and while this year's unit doesn't look elite, they certainly play a more cohesive brand than their predecessors did in 2020. Florida fans (myself included) begged on their hands and knees for Lane Kiffin to come to Gainesville. Ultimately, that didn't work out, and when it was announced that Jon Sumrall was the hire, Gator Nation revolted. For 24 hours, that is. After hearing the man speak and seeing the plan he had in place for the orange and blue, many of the Florida faithful started to have hope. It's early on in the process, but Sumrall and his staff have already started to show proof of concept, winning a road SEC game and then clobbering one of the best teams in the country in back-to-back weeks. I can't say for certain if Jon Sumrall will ever win anything of significance while coaching the Florida Gators. This season is only four games old, and it's year one of his tenure. But with the way things are trending, both on and off the field, it's safe to say football is, at the very least, fun again in The Swamp. I try to be as objective as possible in my writing, but you can read it for yourself in my bio: I'm an unabashed Florida fan. This was an article 17 years in the making, and I want to reiterate that the job is far from finished. The Gators moved all the way up to 8th in the AP Poll on Sunday, their highest position in any poll since the end of the 2020 regular season. No one is going to hang a banner about where you are ranked in week five, and there are plenty more tests still on the schedule. This feels different, though. Will the Gators win an SEC Championship or national title in 2026? Not likely, but I see the vision from Sumrall and trust this is a sustainable approach to building a consistent winner. Florida labored in finding an explosive offense outside of a few years with Mullen, so Sumrall went out and hired the best offensive coordinator in the country in Buster Faulkner. Offensive line play has been downright putrid for large swathes of the last decade and a half, so Sumrall brought offensive line coach and UF alum Phil Trautwein, widely considered the best O-line teacher and recruiter in college football, back to Gainesville. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The man gets it. Sumrall said in his postgame press conference that the beast hasn't been fully awakened yet, a nod to his comments from his introductory press conference back in December, but he acknowledged that they are getting there. And if what I'm hearing from those close to the program is true about the recruits in attendance, the beast might be waking up sooner rather than later. Saying the Gators are "back" feels a bit premature and might be an oversimplification of things, but the fact that they are even in the conversation means things are trending in the right direction. articles.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
articles.summary: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.
articles.body:
"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."

The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.

Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.

It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.

We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.

Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting.

It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire.

"Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.

He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals.

"I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."

He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.

At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach.

"We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.

Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.

The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.

Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.

Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.

We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.

About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.

As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.

We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.

Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.

Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.

Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.

There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line.

"It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.

The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.

Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.

In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.

Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.

She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.

A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.

About 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.

We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.

Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day.

"We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.

Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain.

"We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.

Fatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."

Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.

She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said.

"I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."

A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.

On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.

It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.

articles.title: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents searched U.S. government sites in unexpected ways
articles.summary: AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own.
articles.body: OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount. The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information. Separately, AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed. OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge. AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too. It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now-notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control. In a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, President Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own. The U.S. is not going to be “putting on brakes,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.” The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved. In the Department of Education incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered. In another case involving the Securities and Exchange Commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do. SEC spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed.” The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases.” Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a social media post Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen.” OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

articles.title: Deadly storm hits the Northeast, and five arrested on terrorism charge near a U.S. air base: Weekend Rundown
articles.summary: Nor’easter floods the coast, a major incident is declared at a U.S. air base, and the Knicks on “Saturday Night Live.”
articles.body: A powerful nor’easter battered the Northeast again on Sunday, flooding coastal communities and leaving tens of thousands of homes and businesses without power as forecasters warned that another round of high tides could inundate vulnerable shorelines. The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City Housing Authority worker when a tree fell Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf from New Jersey to New England. The nor’easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy, which left behind over $60 billion in damage across the eastern U.S. in 2012. While this storm’s impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the East Coast this fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that’s disrupting this year’s weather. Hurricane Nolo skirts Hawaii, but powerful winds and flooding remain threats Officials said Hurricane Nolo still posed a risk for flash floods, dangerous winds and extreme surf in areas recovering from previous storms. Nolo was churning very slowly south of the Big Island with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph. Its center was about 165 miles south-southwest of Hawaii’s southernmost point, and it was forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane late Sunday and early Monday while traveling westward to the south of the islands. Five men arrested on terrorism charge near U.S. air base in Britain British police arrested several men on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses on Sunday and evacuated homes near an air base that the U.S. Air Force had been using to facilitate strikes on Iran. A major incident was declared, with a massive emergency presence seen around RAF Fairford, which is about 90 minutes outside London, close to the village of Whelford in west England. The Gloucestershire police force said it responded in the early hours of Sunday to reports of three suspicious vehicles moving toward the base and arrested five men. Asked about the incident, President Donald Trump told reporters the arrest was an “amazing job.” Iran ‘fully prepared’ for war to resume, but diplomacy not over yet, foreign minister says Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said his country is prepared to resume fighting with the United States but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. “We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war,” Araghchi told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, when asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Trump could seek to resume bombing after the U.S. midterm elections. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.” Araghchi told moderator Kristen Welker that despite Trump’s public comments, the rejection had still not been officially communicated to Iran via mediators. He reaffirmed that Iran was ready to reopen the strait as part of an agreement to end the conflict, adding that in return, “we want our monies, our assets, which are illegally frozen, to be released. We want to be able to sell our oil.” Bill Gates says getting global AI regulations will be harder than Cold War-era nuclear negotiations Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates called on the U.S. to be a leader in regulating the growth of artificial intelligence but warned that getting countries to agree on a global framework could be “more difficult” than Cold War-era negotiations to limit nuclear weapons. “This is more difficult than that was,” Gates told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Wednesday during a wide-ranging discussion on AI that aired Sunday. His remarks came as he spoke about Trump’s stance against regulating AI. Gates argued that regulating AI companies by imposing monitoring systems would not hamper the U.S. in any race with China to develop superior technology. In a Sunday interview on “Meet the Press,” Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., said the U.S. and China need to form a working group with technology experts from both countries to come to an agreement on AI. Some lawmakers doubt a Congress that’s ‘barely capable of email’ can regulate AI “A lot of them can’t spell it,” quipped GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego was equally skeptical: “They still don’t know how to get on the internet.” One thing that everyone seems to agree on: Congress is not close to regulating AI. It hasn’t passed any sweeping, comprehensive legislation regulating the internet, invented more than 40 years ago, instead taking a more piecemeal approach and relying on existing laws. New York Knicks’ Jalen Brunson kicks off the new season of ‘SNL’ NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live” with musical guest Katseye. Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during Knicks’ NBA Finals games. “The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.” Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players, Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy. Notable quote An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years. Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance. Hundreds of supporters had gathered outside the building to protest her eviction. The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink. In case you missed it The White House blocked CNN from joining Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday, where it was supposed to cover the president on behalf of major TV networks.A woman Giants announcers dubbed “mom of the year” after cameras caught her carrying a baby and an armful of food back to her seat while a man beside her began eating says the viral clip didn’t show the whole story.A third person has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old woman who police said was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned Mississippi home in August.Carrot Top has been released from the hospital following treatment after a suicide attempt last week, a representative for the comedian confirmed to NBC News.Another woman’s body was found near Johannesburg, bringing to 10 the number of victims in a series of killings under investigation, South African police said.

articles.title: Powerful storm floods US Northeast, causes power outages
articles.summary: The nor’easter causes another round of flooding in low-lying areas in New Jersey and New York City and knocks out power.
articles.body:
A powerful storm is pummelling the shoreline in the northeastern United States for a second day, causing another round of flooding in low-lying areas and knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes.

Tidal surges swamped low-lying neighbourhoods in New Jersey on Sunday, while wind gusts toppled trees on New York’s Long Island, damaging homes and bringing down utility poles.

In New York City, streets in the Howard Beach neighbourhood of Queens were inundated.

The slow-moving storm , which killed a New York City housing authority worker when a tree fell on Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday, with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf all the way to New England.

Extreme amounts of rain – more than 10cm (4 inches) since Friday in some spots in New Jersey – combined with a surging ocean led to flooding amounts not seen for close to a decade in places used to dealing with high water, residents said.

The storm, known as a nor’easter, triggered memories of Hurricane Sandy , which left behind more than $60bn in damage across the eastern US in 2012. While this storm’s impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the East Coast this fall because of an El Nino climate pattern disrupting this year’s weather.

Images of waves crashing into sea walls and onto beaches raised concerns about coastal erosion.

More than 100,000 customers were without power across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic at times on Sunday, according to PowerOutage.us. The most widespread outages were in counties along the coast from New Jersey to Connecticut.

Numerous flights were cancelled or delayed up and down the coast. More than 250 flights had been cancelled at Boston Logan International airport by late Sunday morning as wind gusts reached 64km/hour (40 mph), according to the Massachusetts Port Authority.

The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected on Sunday from northern New Jersey into southern New England.

While the storm was gradually weakening, tidal flooding would stay through high-tide cycles Sunday night, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.
